cards.headline: Iran denies responsibility for drone strikes in Kuwait that killed two Italians

pages.text: Iran denied involvement on November 26, 2026, in drone strikes against military facilities in Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the Italian Senate that several Iranian drones struck Kuwaiti military sites at approximately 2 pm local time, including an air defence radar centre. Two Italian specialists employed by the arms company Rheinmetall were working at the site when the attack occurred. Following the incident, Kuwait's foreign ministry summoned Iran's ambassador in response to what it described as “continued Iranian attacks.”

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the accusations baseless and held telephone conversations with both Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah and Antonio Tajani to deny Tehran's role. Araghchi proposed a joint investigation with Rome and Kuwait City to determine the cause of the incident, later stating on X that the event looked like a “precooked recipe for war.” Abolfazl Shekarchi, a senior spokesperson for Iran's armed forces, also denied any Iranian military operation in the region, accusing the United States and Israel of staging a false flag attack to destabilize the area. Additionally, the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency cited an unnamed security source alleging that Ukraine had deployed a network of thousands of drones across the region, including in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.

The attack drew condemnation from the UAE, Syria, Jordan, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who called for increased pressure on Tehran. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also condemned the strike and called for restraint. Kuwait's Al-Sabah condemned the strike as “a heinous Iranian aggression.” While Iran has repeatedly struck Arab Gulf states with drones and missiles since the start of the war, targeting military bases and US-linked facilities, the Iranian army confirmed a separate drone attack on Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base earlier in November.

cards.headline: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte to face ICC trial over war on drugs

pages.text: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30. He faces three counts of crimes against humanity related to his anti-narcotics campaign. For the families of the thousands killed during the drug war, the proceedings represent a chance for justice that has been unavailable within the Philippines. The trial also serves as a test for the ICC, which faces political pressure and questions regarding its capacity to hold former heads of state accountable.

Duterte, 81, remains a popular figure in the Philippines, where many view his violent crackdown as a major presidential achievement. His daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, is a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, meaning the ICC proceedings could become a defining issue in that election and impact the political fortunes of the Duterte dynasty. Duterte was elected president in 2016 following a populist campaign in which he promised to kill criminals and drug dealers. During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he was credited with making the city safer, though human rights groups reported systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad. ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee that group.

cards.headline: At least eight migrants found dead on boat near Spain’s Canary Islands

pages.text: At least eight migrants were found dead on a boat carrying approximately 100 people that was rescued near Spain’s Canary Islands, according to the Spanish maritime rescue service. On November 27, 2026, the Spanish news agency EFE reported that 14 bodies had been brought ashore. The maritime rescue service had previously stated that between eight and 10 bodies were found on board and that six people were airlifted to a hospital in serious condition. The boat was discovered 39 nautical miles (72km) south of the island of El Hierro and was being towed to the port of La Estaca. Separately, 84 survivors from another boat arrived at La Restinga, the main port of El Hierro, which contains a migrant reception centre and field hospital.

The Canary Islands are a Spanish region in the Atlantic Ocean located off the coast of northwest Africa. Because anyone landing there reaches Spanish and European Union territory, the islands serve as a primary entry point for migrants from West Africa. Migrant arrivals to the islands have accelerated since October, hitting a record of 2,100 people in a single day on November 25, most of whom arrived on El Hierro, an island with 11,400 residents. Authorities on the island previously declared an emergency, and rescuers brought in nearly 1,500 people in a single day on November 14. In 2024, arrivals reached a record of more than 46,000 before falling following tighter surveillance and cooperation with countries of origin and transit.

Patrols off Senegal, Mauritania, and Morocco have pushed departures further south to The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Guinea, which makes the Atlantic crossing longer and more dangerous. Regional leader Fernando Clavijo expressed a feeling of impotence over the tragedy on X, stating, “The humanitarian emergency doesn’t start on El Hierro, but on the shores of Senegal and Gambia, where we have to act.” He called for action from the Spanish government and the European Commission. The deaths occur as immigration has emerged as a defining campaign issue in Spain ahead of a general election. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is an advocate of the economic benefits of immigration, while the right-wing, which leads in opinion polls, seeks tighter controls.

cards.headline: At least 31 killed in fuel tanker fire on Cairo's Ring Road

pages.text: A fuel tanker crash sparked a massive fire on the Ring Road in the Waraq district of Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, on November 25, 2026. Egyptian authorities said the blaze killed at least 31 people and injured at least 21 others. The Health Ministry reported that the fire left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred. Rescue workers were seen pulling people from burning vehicles at the scene in the densely populated neighborhood. Families and local residents recently gathered outside Al Salam Mosque in Waraq to bid farewell to the victims, including five members of a single family: a father, his daughter, his son, and two nephews.

cards.headline: Russian military flotillas turn around in Mediterranean after warship sunk in Libya

pages.text: A convoy of Russian ships carrying military vehicles bound for Libya has turned around in the Mediterranean following a Ukrainian maritime drone attack that sank a Russian naval corvette in Benghazi port on November 22, according to three people from military and security services told Reuters. The sinking occurred approximately 2,000 km (1,240 miles) from the battlefield in Ukraine. The Russian defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the incident.

A European military official tracking the movements reported that another convoy, escorted by the Russian navy frigate Golovko, turned around near the Strait of Sicily on the same day as the attack in Benghazi. The Strait of Sicily serves as a key point before the North African coast. Additionally, a Ukrainian military intelligence official and a Middle East security official confirmed that a second flotilla had turned from heading to Libya and is now paused off the coast of Algeria.

cards.headline: Manitoba premier calls upheld Quebec religious symbols law 'legislative racism'

pages.text: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew has condemned a Quebec law that bars certain public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols, calling the legislation an act of “legislative racism.” The criticism follows a 6-1 ruling by Canada’s Supreme Court that largely upheld Quebec's Bill 21, a secularism law passed in 2019. Kinew stated the law was “designed to discriminate” primarily against Muslims, but also Sikhs and other religious minorities. He argued that Canadians who believe in equality must speak up against the use of constitutional mechanisms to erode minority rights, noting that he wants a Canada where an RCMP officer can wear a turban and a teacher can wear a hijab if she chooses. Kinew also mentioned that a Hutterite woman should be able to wear a head covering and a person should be able to wear a cross.

The Supreme Court's decision centered on the province's use of the “notwithstanding clause,” a mechanism in Section 33 of the Charter that allows provincial or federal governments to adopt laws even if courts determine they are unconstitutional. This clause allows governments to override certain fundamental rights, such as religious freedom, equality, and speech, for up to five years at a time before needing to face voters for renewal. In the majority opinion, Chief Justice Richard Wagner wrote that Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s “legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society.” The court found that the Quebec government properly invoked the clause to shield the law from challenges. While most of the law was upheld, the court struck down a prohibition that prevented members of the province's legislature from wearing face coverings. The justices noted that while the law is upheld, judges can still declare that laws protected by the clause have violated the Charter, a finding they said would be useful for voters and legislators.

Bill 21 prohibits various public-sector workers, including lawyers, judges, police, and teachers, from wearing conspicuous religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah, or a cross while on the job. The Supreme Court ruling has drawn conflicting reactions. Some in Quebec celebrated the decision as a vindication of the province's position. However, religious civil liberties groups criticized the outcome. Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters that the ability of governments to take away the rights of minority groups because it is popular prevents the country from having a true charter of rights and freedoms, describing it instead as a “charter of suggestions and permissions.” The Supreme Court noted that the four days of hearings for this case marked one of the longest in its 151-year history, involving 51 interveners, including a record six attorneys general.

cards.headline: At least 13 Nigerien guards killed in attack in Tillaberi region

pages.text: At least 13 members of the Nigerien National Guard were killed and 20 others wounded during a terrorist attack in the village of Sanam, located in the Tillaberi region of western Niger, on November 26, 2026. The Nigerien defence ministry reported that a large group of heavily armed assailants targeted the National Guard position, which was part of an anti-jihadist operation. While the ministry described the attackers as terrorists without naming a specific group, Daesh claimed responsibility for the attack on its Telegram channel. The ministry stated that several militants were “neutralized” and their logistical equipment was destroyed, and that a search is underway to track down the remaining assailants. The casualty figures provided by the ministry are provisional, and the most seriously wounded soldiers have been evacuated for medical treatment.

The Tillaberi region, situated on the borders with Mali and Burkina Faso, has become the epicenter of jihadist attacks in Niger. According to the conflict monitor ACLED, Tillaberi was the deadliest region in the central Sahel in 2025, where civilians were the primary targets. ACLED attributed the increase in violence to the region's strategic location in the tri-border area, a flashpoint zone where the frontiers of Niger, Burkina Faso, and Mali converge and where jihadists operate. This follows another incident on November 12, when at least 37 civilians were killed in an ambush by unidentified armed men near the city of Tera in the Tillaberi region. Additionally, 11 soldiers were killed in Baraoua, in the eastern Diffa region. Niger also faces violence from Boko Haram and its dissident branch, the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), in the Lake Chad basin near the Nigerian border in the southeast.

Niger has been ruled by a military junta since a 2023 coup and continues to battle violence from jihadist groups linked to Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State. These conflicts have resulted in thousands of deaths over the last decade. Within the country's armed forces, repeated battlefield losses have fueled tensions, which culminated in a failed mutiny in late August.

cards.headline: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez makes final campaign appeal before November 29 election

pages.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez held a final rally in Madrid on November 27, 2026, urging citizens to vote in large numbers to prevent the country from going “backwards.” The Socialist leader's appeal comes ahead of the general election scheduled for November 29, 2026. Sanchez told supporters that the elections are about moving Spain forward and warned that a right-wing coalition government including far-right members in parliament would gut public services and reverse years of social progress.

Opinion polls suggest the election could end Sanchez's eight years of leftist leadership. The conservative People's Party (PP) is slated to come out on top according to polls, though the PP may need to rely on support from the far-right anti-immigration Vox party to form a government. There is also a possibility of a hung parliament, a situation where neither the left bloc nor the right-wing coalition secures a majority.

Sanchez has campaigned on his record of boosting the Spanish economy while European Union partners struggled, specifically citing policies that increased the minimum wage and raised pensions in line with inflation. However, voters have expressed frustration over a soaring cost of living and high rental prices that prevent many from leaving their parents' homes, despite reported economic growth.

cards.headline: Son of Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi expresses relief after first call in five years

pages.text: Kim Aris, the son of Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi, said he was relieved to hear his mother's voice for the first time in five years, though he questioned if the military's gesture was genuine. The 81-year-old Suu Kyi, who served as Myanmar's de facto head of government following a 2020 election victory, was recently moved by the military to house arrest at an undisclosed location. Aris told Euronews' The World Conversation that while he was happy to know she is alive and well, he remains concerned about her condition. He noted that for two or three years, the family had not known if she was alive. The call, which was recorded and monitored and focused on family matters, occurred after the Myanmar embassy in London contacted the British Foreign Office the week before it took place. Aris, a British citizen, has campaigned for his mother's release since the military seized power in February 2021 by speaking at universities and meeting with governments. He previously ran a proof-of-life campaign, and the Red Cross visited Suu Kyi to confirm she was alive. Aris disputed the military's use of the term 'house arrest,' stating she is not in her own home and has no access to media. He said she had previously been held in solitary confinement in a prison in the capital, Naypyidaw, with contact limited to military or police personnel and military doctors.

cards.headline: CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, and Telus to stop charging prohibited fees

pages.text: Canada's telecommunications regulator, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC), has ordered Bell, Rogers, and Telus to stop charging certain consumer fees that violate the Telecommunications Act. The companies must cease these charges by December. The regulator's decision follows a June ban on fees used to activate, change, or cancel internet and cellphone services. After that ban, major carriers introduced hardware-related and SIM card charges that the CRTC flagged as potential disguised activation fees. SIM cards are microchips required to connect a device to a mobile network. Sheehan Carter, the CRTC's acting vice-president of consumer analytics and strategy, told reporters at a virtual briefing that the regulator identified fees from the largest telephone companies that appeared to be prohibited. Carter stated that because the companies continued the fees and argued they were not prohibited, the CRTC took action to decide the issue.

The CRTC ruled that specific charges related to providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for service plans are prohibited. These include a cellphone handling charge from Bell, a cellphone setup charge from Rogers, and a SIM and eSIM provisioning fee from Telus. However, the regulator ruled that fees charged by Rogers and Telus to replace broken or lost SIM cards are not prohibited, and Rogers' shipping fees are also permitted. Separately, the CRTC has threatened Bell with a fine of up to $10 million for allegedly violating wireless rules by selling customers cellphones locked to its network. In a statement to CBC News, a Rogers spokesperson said the company disagrees with the CRTC's position on device set-up charges, arguing those charges help recover real costs, though the spokesperson noted the company is pleased the CRTC's decision regarding shipping and SIM replacement fees reflects this.

cards.headline: New Zealand election results show incumbent coalition lacks majority

pages.text: Final results from New Zealand’s general election indicate that the incumbent right-wing coalition will require support from the centrist newcomer Opportunity party to form a government and avoid a new election. The National-led bloc currently holds 65 seats in the 130-seat parliament, falling one seat short of the 66 seats required for a majority. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon must now negotiate with Opportunity to remain in power, which holds seven seats. If a deal cannot be reached, the country will likely need to hold another election. The final tally followed the release of results from nearly 485,000 “special votes,” which are ballots cast from overseas or outside a voter’s specific electorate.

The revised seat counts following the special votes are as follows: National has 40 seats, Labour has 36, the Greens have 17, Act has 13, New Zealand First has 12, Opportunity has seven, and Te Pati Māori has five. While preliminary results on 7 November had suggested the National party and its two coalition partners—the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties—held a slim two-seat majority, the final count changed the landscape. Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes were tallied: Labour won Wairarapa from National by 81 votes and took Hamilton East from National by 173 votes, while the Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour by 1,610 votes. National could potentially return to power with a slim majority without needing Opportunity if it applies for a recount and wins back at least one of those seats.

cards.headline: Civil society organisations in Ghana reject proposed five-year presidential and parliamentary terms

pages.text: Civil society organisations (CSOs) in Ghana have rejected a proposal to extend presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years. The groups also demanded changes to government proposals regarding the election of Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), insisting that citizens must be allowed to elect local government leaders without presidential interference. These positions followed a two-day engagement between the Constitutional Reform Implementation Committee (CREC) and more than 100 CSOs aimed at building consensus on proposed amendments to Ghana’s 1992 Constitution. The CSOs argued that the current four-year mandate, which permits a president to seek a second term, provides sufficient time for elected officials to implement governance programmes.

Oliver Barker-Vormawor, the Executive Secretary of the CREC, stated that the engagement resulted in significant progress, noting that CSOs agreed with approximately 89 per cent of the government’s proposed reforms. The discussions reduced the number of outstanding issues from an initial 41 to 10. Barker-Vormawor explained that unresolved matters, including the proposed term extension and a demand that Members of Parliament (MPs) not serve as ministers, will be referred back to Cabinet for possible reconsideration. He clarified that the CREC's responsibility is to communicate stakeholder concerns to Cabinet, which serves as the decision-maker, rather than independently altering the government's position.

cards.headline: Voters in Taiwan cast ballots in local elections amid concerns of Chinese interference

pages.text: Voters in Taiwan began casting ballots on November 28, 2026, to elect mayors, council members, and other local leaders across 22 cities and counties. The elections, often referred to as “nine-in-one” elections because they contest nine categories of local government posts, involve approximately 11,000 positions. Winners will serve four-year terms. While campaigns have primarily focused on local issues such as transport, childcare, housing affordability, the environment, and wealth distribution, the vote is being closely watched due to tensions with China. Beijing, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island, has repeatedly weighed in on the process. Taiwanese officials have raised alarms regarding thousands of suspected incidents of election interference and misinformation, including reports of hundreds of China-linked, AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about politicians disliked by Beijing. China’s Taiwan affairs office spokesperson, Zhu Fenglian, has called these allegations “completely fabricated,” stating they “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes.”

The elections feature intense competition between the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the main opposition Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT has traditionally performed better in local elections and favors closer ties with Beijing. In Taipei, a traditional KMT stronghold, incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an faces a challenge from DPP national legislator Puma Shen. Shen, an academic and expert on China’s information warfare, was declared a “diehard separatist” by Beijing in 2024, and Chinese police say he is wanted for “separatism.” In New Taipei City, Taiwan’s most populous city, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is challenging the KMT incumbent. Other notable races include Kaohsiung in the south, where the mayoral office is currently held by the DPP. President Lai Ching-te has campaigned for DPP candidates, including at a rally in New Taipei City. Political scientist Wei-Ting Yen of Academia Sinica noted that while local elections are not primarily about China, the outcome will have significant implications for cross-strait relations.

cards.headline: Ontario gaming minister seeks to tighten online gambling ad regulations

pages.text: Ontario Minister of Tourism, Culture and Gaming Zee Hamid said the province is doing everything possible to improve regulations for online gaming advertisements. Hamid's comments followed statements from Premier Doug Ford, who described the advertisements as being “out of control.” Speaking at a news conference on November 24, 2026, Hamid stated, “I agree with the premier,” and noted concerns regarding the rise in gambling addiction and problematic gambling. Ford previously told reporters at Queen's Park that he has asked his cabinet to investigate online gambling advertisements.

The government is facing pressure from opposition Members of Provincial Parliament (MPPs) to implement a ban on most online gambling advertisements by the end of the year. These opposition members are calling for the ban to be enacted without waiting for a cabinet report on the matter. In May, the Ford government struck down a Liberal bill that had proposed a ban on most online gambling advertisements. Hamid defended that decision, stating that a report outlining the pros and cons of the issue is necessary to ensure new regulations do not cause further harm, such as driving users toward an unregulated “grey market” of illegitimate platforms.

Ontario's regulated online gaming market was launched in 2022 under the Ford government. Prior to that launch, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) was the only internet gaming site regulated under the province's alcohol and gaming commission.

cards.headline: Capsized tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed from Ibiza

pages.text: Spanish officials say the Malta-registered tanker Med Emre, which capsized off the island of Ibiza on December 3, 2026, will be towed to the port of Cartagena. The vessel is carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel. The Spanish transport ministry stated that Cartagena is the only port that meets the technical requirements necessary to perform repair work and extract the cargo. The operation to move the ship is being described as a challenging rescue mission. While there were initial concerns regarding a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean, an inspection indicated that the ship's fuel tanks remain intact. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told the Cadena SER radio network that current information suggests a leak is not occurring, expressing hope that the tanker could reach port in the coming hours or days.

The Med Emre was traveling from Algeciras, near Gibraltar, to Barcelona when the incident occurred. Following the capsize, all 17 crew members were rescued, though the chief engineer later died in a hospital. Six people received treatment for minor injuries. An investigation into the cause of the incident is currently underway. To monitor for environmental impact, the Clara Campoamor—a pollution control vessel owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service—is assessing any possible damage by air and sea. Spanish authorities have not provided specific details regarding the process for extracting the diesel from the vessel.

cards.headline: Storms cause flooding, power outages, and travel disruptions across the United States during Thanksgiving

pages.text: Heavy rain, strong winds, and snow disrupted holiday travel and caused widespread damage across the United States during Thanksgiving. The storms led to water rescues from New York to Virginia, downed trees and power lines, and significant disruptions to air and rail travel. In New Jersey, widespread flooding reached levels not seen since 2012, following Hurricane Sandy. Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency for all of New Jersey, while Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for parts of New York. In New Jersey's Sea Isle City and Ocean City, streets were inundated, and water spread across parts of Avalon. Scott J. Wahl, the Borough of Avalon business administrator, stated the town was experiencing some of the worst flooding in its history. Wahl reported that a few drivers had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into floodwaters, though no injuries were reported. In New York City, strong winds and flooding disrupted train lines, toppled trees, and caused scaffolding structures to collapse, though no injuries were reported. Zohran Mamdani noted that several people had to be rescued from their cars amid flooding in the city.

cards.headline: Saudi air strikes kill 11 civilians in Yemen’s Taiz governorate, Houthi media reports

pages.text: Houthi-affiliated news media reported on November 27, 2026, that Saudi air strikes killed 11 civilians in the city of al-Turbah, located south of the provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen. According to the Saba news agency, which is affiliated with the Houthi armed group, the raid targeted a residential building. A local source told the agency that most of the victims were children. Rescue teams retrieved eight bodies from the site, while three people remain missing beneath the rubble. Al Jazeera could not independently verify these reports. The Saudi Arabia-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemen government, did not immediately comment on the alleged strike. The coalition later stated that it had destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis toward the Riyadh region of Saudi Arabia.

The reported strike occurs amid ongoing hostilities between the Iran-backed Houthi group and government forces supported by a Saudi-led military coalition. Yemen has experienced violence since the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and other regions in 2014, leading to the formation of the Saudi-led coalition in March 2015. Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July following the collapse of a 2022 ceasefire. Houthi forces have been targeting Saudi Arabia almost daily, hitting airports, energy facilities, and the financial district of Riyadh. These incidents follow a Houthi attack on a Saudi oil refinery reported a day prior to the November 27 strike.

cards.headline: Algeria condemns spillover of Ukraine war into Libya

pages.text: Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf stated on November 26, 2026, that the country opposes the spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war into Libya. Attaf's comments followed a deadly attack by Kyiv on two Russian ships off the eastern city of Benghazi and drone strikes on November 22, 2026, that killed two Libyan soldiers. Attaf said the ship attacks could “only be condemned” and described the drone strikes as a reminder of the need for a solution to the Libyan crisis. He called for an inclusive political process to create unified, legitimate institutions that are “free from foreign dictates.”

Libya is currently divided between a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east. The eastern administration is backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, who has maintained close ties with Russia and the United Arab Emirates. Attaf noted that the political divide in Libya is deep on all levels and stated that issues in Libya and the Sahel region are “interconnected.” He identified foreign interference as Algeria's “main source of concern,” though he did not name specific countries. While Algiers has frequently accused the United Arab Emirates of meddling in the region, Algeria severed diplomatic ties with the Gulf country in September. In an unprecedented move, the Algerian parliament also approved deploying troops to Niger to protect energy installations near the shared border, though reports indicated these troops would be housed in a base in Madama, a desert area closer to southern Libya.

cards.headline: Uganda to withdraw troops from Lubero, DR Congo, within two weeks

pages.text: Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from the town of Lubero in North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), within two weeks. The Ugandan army stated the troops will hand over security in the town to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations. The planned withdrawal applies only to Lubero and follows escalating diplomatic tensions between the two neighbors. While the Ugandan military did not provide a reason for the withdrawal or state if it is linked to the diplomatic row, the announcement comes after the DRC summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa regarding controversial social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the son of President Yoweri Museveni. On November 23, 2026, Kainerugaba threatened on X to take control of the strategic Congolese town of Walikale in North Kivu and called for the unconditional surrender of the airport in Isiro, the provincial capital in Haut-Uele. The DRC responded the following day by summoning the Ugandan diplomat, stating it is determined to ensure respect for its dignity and institutions against provocation or interference.

The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), an Islamist group affiliated with the Islamic State. The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries. Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, in November 2021 following bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala. Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said Operation Shujaa would continue elsewhere in DR Congo. In a separate post on X, Magezi accused militia forces, including some apparently allied to the Congolese government, of increasing attacks on vulnerable communities, specifically mentioning the massacre of women and children from the Bahema and Tutsi communities in Ituri and the North Kivu region. Magezi stated that under International Humanitarian Law (IHL), the UPDF retains the responsibility to extend protection to such communities whenever possible.

Despite the joint offensive, the ADF remains the deadliest armed group in DR Congo. According to the conflict monitoring organisation Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled), the group has killed an average of four civilians a day and expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo. John Ngono, an Acled analyst for DR Congo, noted that findings suggest Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC. The eastern region of DR Congo has experienced violence for more than 30 years, often involving neighbors Uganda and Rwanda. In addition to the ADF, the Congolese army is fighting the FRN anti-governmental group, formerly known as M23, which is backed by Rwanda. cards.headline: B.C. Supreme Court upholds exemption allowing religious health-care facilities to ban MAID

pages.text: The B.C. Supreme Court has upheld an exemption that allows religious health-care facilities to prohibit medical assistance in dying (MAID) on their premises. In a decision from Chief Justice Ronald Skolrood, the court ruled that facilities such as Vancouver’s St. Paul’s Hospital can continue to require patients seeking MAID to transfer to another facility to receive the procedure. St. Paul’s Hospital is operated by the Providence Health Care Society, a Catholic organization that does not permit MAID on its site.

The legal challenge involved three plaintiffs: Gaye, the mother of Samantha O’Neill; Dying With Dignity Canada; and a doctor. The case centered on the experience of Samantha O’Neill, who suffered from Stage 4 cervical cancer and was required to be transferred out of St. Paul’s Hospital in April 2023 to receive MAID in her final hours. Gaye and Jim, O’Neill’s father, stated that the necessity of the transfer denied them the opportunity to say a meaningful and dignified goodbye to their daughter, noting the last time they saw her conscious, she was seated on a commode.

cards.headline: Venezuela to repeal law barring opposition figures from office

pages.text: Venezuela will repeal a law that prohibits opposition figures from assuming public office, according to National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodríguez. The announcement, made on November 26, 2026, follows political transition talks between Venezuela's interim government and parts of the opposition selected by Washington. Rodríguez stated that the legislation, known as the Simón Bolívar Law, responded to a specific situation the country was experiencing and that no politician had been subjected to its provisions. He expressed expectation that the reforms would be approved. The law was passed in 2024 following elections in which Nicolás Maduro was declared the winner despite widespread allegations of fraud. Under the legislation, individuals who requested or supported foreign sanctions against Venezuela faced permanent bans from political office and the confiscation of their assets. The law has been criticized for enabling political persecution.

The proposed repeal comes as Venezuela undergoes a political transition. An interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, the sister of Jorge Rodríguez, has governed the country since January, when Maduro was seized by United States forces. In September, Delcy Rodríguez told the United Nations that the South American nation would hold free and fair elections, though no date has been set. Since August, the interim government and portions of the opposition have been negotiating a “route map towards democracy,” which includes an agreement to review several laws, including the Simón Bolívar Law. This follows the return of Nobel Peace Prize laureate and opposition leader María Corina Machado to Venezuela in October after more than 10 months in exile. Although Machado was legally barred from running in the 2024 election, she is widely expected to run for office in a future election despite her exclusion from the current transition talks.

cards.headline: Guinea-Bissau military leaders delay elections until 2028

pages.text: Military rulers in Guinea-Bissau have postponed the country's presidential and parliamentary elections by two years, delaying the promised return to civilian rule. cards.headline: One in eight children in Gaza is stunted amid war and blockade

pages.text: One in eight children in Gaza is suffering from stunting, a condition where many children have bones that have not matured as they should. In Khan Younis, Gaza, seven-year-old Nabigha al-Zaqzouq stands 99cm (3.2ft) tall and weighs 10kg (22lb), making her appear several years younger than her actual age. Her mother, Alia, reports that while the family lived through extremely harsh days during the war, they are now living under a suffocating blockade following a ceasefire. Alia has noted that meat, fruit, and vegetables are beyond the family's means, leaving bread and canned food as the primary dietary options. She has also struggled to afford the medicines and medical tests required to monitor Nabigha's growth.

The growth issues are affecting multiple children in the region. Five-year-old Tala Zidan is 94cm (3ft) tall, which is approximately 15-16cm shorter than the average for children her age. Alia has observed other children with similar growth problems during medical visits. According to Alia, treatment and medicines are difficult to find and afford, leading her to call for the allowance of medicines and treatments into the area.

cards.headline: CHRAJ dismisses corruption and conflict of interest complaints against President Mahama and others

pages.text: The Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ) has dismissed a complaint alleging corruption, abuse of power, and conflict of interest involving President John Dramani Mahama, Vice President Prof Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, and businessman Ibrahim Mahama in Ghana. In a decision dated November 25, 2026, CHRAJ stated that investigations did not establish wrongdoing regarding the acquisition of the Damang Gold Mine by Engineers and Planners (E&P), a company owned by Ibrahim Mahama, or the use of his private aircraft for official travels. The complaint was filed by Emmanuel Senyo Amekplenu, who raised concerns that family relationships and private benefits might have influenced government decisions.

Regarding the Damang Gold Mine, Amekplenu questioned if President Mahama influenced Cabinet deliberations, as the transaction benefited his brother, Ibrahim Mahama, through E&P. However, CHRAJ found that the President recused himself from the March 18, 2026, Cabinet meeting where the matter was discussed. The Commission noted that Vice President Opoku-Agyemang informed the Cabinet of the President's recusal on conflict-of-interest grounds and presided over that meeting. CHRAJ also established that the acquisition process began under the previous New Patriotic Party administration, when the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources issued a no-objection letter to E&P in March 2024 to explore the potential acquisition. The subsequent award followed a competitive bidding process administered by the Minerals Commission, with E&P emerging as the successful bidder. CHRAJ noted that while Ibrahim Mahama is the beneficial owner of E&P, the company is a separate legal entity from him.

The complaint also addressed the use of Ibrahim Mahama’s private jet for presidential travels and for transporting the Vice President abroad for medical treatment in 2025, citing concerns about undue influence and reciprocity. CHRAJ concluded there was no evidence the aircraft arrangement imposed any cost on the state or influenced the President's official duties. The Commission determined the provision of the aircraft could be considered a family-related benefit, which is not prohibited under its conflict of interest guidelines as long as it does not influence official duties. The CHRAJ statement was signed by Dr Joseph Whittal.

cards.headline: Global cybercrime network known as 'the Com' poses threat to children

pages.text: Crime agencies worldwide warn that a sprawling and fluid global network of online communities, known as the Com (short for the Community), is being used by young cybercriminals to target children. The FBI estimates that thousands of people identify as members, or recent members, of the group. While the name sounds benign, authorities say the network is linked to activities including the distribution of indecent images of girls and blackmail. Typical members are described as boys or young men aged 16 to 25, who are primarily native English speakers.

The criminal activities associated with the Com are broad, ranging from data theft and cryptocurrency scams to bringing down IT systems and launching attacks that slow down networks. Beyond digital disruption, some members target vulnerable young girls by encouraging them to harm themselves or sacrifice their pets. In these cases, criminals may coerce girls into taking indecent images of themselves to share. Victims are often threatened with doxing or swatting, a practice where fictitious incidents are reported to emergency services at a victim's address to trigger a response from authorities, sometimes armed officers.

In the United Kingdom, a judge jailed Beau-Jack Mensforth for his activities as part of the Com. Mensforth operated from his bedroom in north-east England, representing one individual in a group that police believe likely includes thousands more. Because of these risks, police are urging parents to be aware of these activities and to check their children's devices.

cards.headline: Suspected North Korean operative used fake Toronto IT company to secure remote jobs

pages.text: An individual using the name Aku Alatao, who presented himself as the founder and CEO of Toronto-based Neiluno Software, is a suspected North Korean operative working under a false Canadian identity. An investigation by CBC's Fifth Estate found that Alatao and multiple other suspected North Korean operatives have posed online as Canadian residents to secure remote jobs at Canadian companies and within the government. These paycheques are used to support the heavily sanctioned North Korean regime.

During an online job interview this past summer, Alatao applied for a position with the Canadian startup Bananacoin to create a cryptocurrency and design a website. Alatao's resumé included extensive previous front- and back-end coding experience, and he proposed working remotely. Bananacoin executive Clark Shelley questioned Alatao about the company name during the interview, to which Alatao replied, “Yeah, maybe it is very good.” The company offered Alatao a starting salary of $8,000 per month, though the investigation found that neither Alatao nor Bananacoin were real.

cards.headline: Newly identified prehistoric hyena species found in China

pages.text: Researchers have identified a new species of prehistoric hyena, *Dinocrocuta yingliangi*, from the Linxia Basin in northwestern China. Found in deposits dated to roughly 11.2 million–9.8 million years ago, the species is the earliest known member of the lineage that includes *Dinocrocuta gigantea*, the largest known bone-cracking hyena. This discovery helps trace the origins of the lion-sized predator, as the earlier history of *D. gigantea* has been difficult to reconstruct despite its fossils being abundant in younger deposits in the Linxia Basin. Qigao Jiangzuo of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and colleagues described the findings in the journal *Palaeontology*.

The partial skull of *D. yingliangi* provides evidence that adaptations for slicing meat and hunting were already present early in this lineage's history. Additionally, the skull records a remarkable recovery: the animal lost a canine tooth and survived long enough for bone to fill the socket. The fossils were discovered on the northeastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau.

cards.headline: Rising costs and reduced aid drive hunger in northern Yemen despite food availability

pages.text: Families in Houthi-controlled areas of northern Yemen are facing hunger because rising food prices, scarce employment, and the suspension of food aid have made basic goods unaffordable, even though items like flour and oil remain available in markets in cities such as Hodeidah and Sanaa. According to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report, a humanitarian and food security assessment, food was available in markets that monitors could reach in September, but families had less money to spend. In Houthi-controlled areas like Hodeidah, the cost of a basket of basic foods in September was approximately 7 percent, or $91, more than in August, marking its highest level in a year. While the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) reports that prices are rising faster in the government-held south, families in the north face specific challenges regarding income and assistance. FEWS NET reported in October that most households in and around northern towns find only five to 10 days of paid work per month. Additionally, FEWS NET stated that the UN World Food Programme’s (WFP) food assistance in Houthi-held areas has been suspended since September 2025.

The economic pressure has forced residents to alter how they purchase necessities. Umm Sami, a widow raising four children in the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, sells household goods and performs occasional domestic work to feed her family. She told Al Jazeera that rising prices have changed her shopping habits, noting that she sometimes buys only enough flour or oil to last one day because she cannot afford a whole bag.

cards.headline: Ghana Education Ministry sued over two-year ban on early examination candidates

pages.text: Private legal practitioner Shafic Osman has filed an application for judicial review at the High Court in Accra, challenging a directive from the Ghana Education Ministry that imposes a two-year examination ban on students who sit the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) or West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE) ahead of the approved schedule. The directive was communicated by the Ghana Education Service (GES) on November 23, 2026. Mr. Osman is asking the court to quash the decision and declare that the Education Minister's authority to issue policy directives does not extend to imposing such a mandatory ban without further lawful authority. The application names the Minister for Education and the Ghana Education Service as the first and second respondents, with the West African Examinations Council (WAEC) listed as an interested party.

In an affidavit supporting the application, Mr. Osman argues that the prohibition is unlawful and ultra vires, meaning it exceeds the legal power of the Ministry. He contends that the directive introduces a punitive disqualification not authorized by existing statutory or examination regulatory frameworks. Mr. Osman points to WAEC’s 2023 Rules and Regulations for Dealing with Cases of Irregularity in the Council’s Examinations, which already provide mechanisms for addressing irregularities. These existing rules include provisions for the registration of unqualified candidates, falsification of continuous assessment records, disciplinary referrals for school officials, the possible de-recognition of schools for at least one year, and the withholding or cancellation of examination results following investigations by a WAEC committee. Mr. Osman argues that these rules do not prescribe a two-year prohibition on future examination participation for candidates who were prematurely registered or sat an exam before becoming eligible.

The legal challenge also raises concerns regarding the absence of procedural safeguards and individual investigations under the new directive. Mr. Osman argues that the policy fails to distinguish between a candidate who knowingly participates in an examination irregularity and a candidate whose premature registration results from the error or misconduct of another person.

cards.headline: New deep-sea fish species identified from specimen eaten 42 years ago

pages.text: A single specimen found in the stomach contents of a predatory fish has been identified as a new species of deep-sea cardinalfish. The specimen was originally part of a beardfish caught in July 1984 at an estimated depth of 370-450 meters (1,210-1,480 feet) off Kita-iwo Island in Japan’s Ogasawara Islands. The specimen remained in a Tokyo museum collection for 42 years before being examined by museum staff and volunteers. The newly described species, Epigonus masamunei, measures approximately 8 centimeters (3 inches) from snout to tail base and possesses large eyes, a common trait for fish living in dark deep-sea environments. Because no one has seen the species alive, its color remains unknown.

The discovery was led by Makoto Okamoto, a fish taxonomist at the Japan Fisheries Research and Education Agency. Okamoto noted that it is rare for new species of deep-sea fish to be discovered through this process. The species was named Epigonus masamunei after Masamune, a medieval Japanese swordsmith, because the curve of the fish's spine resembles the swords produced by the smith. The predator that consumed the specimen was a beardfish (Polymixia japonica), a larger deep-sea fish that commonly grows to about 20 cm (8 in) long. Damage to the specimen's belly, skin, and the tips of some fin spines suggests the beardfish may have vomited the cardinalfish back up.

cards.headline: Abetifi District Hospital in Ghana remains abandoned 11 years after project award

pages.text: The Abetifi District Hospital in the Kwahu East District of Ghana remains incomplete and abandoned, 11 years after it was awarded as part of a six-hospital turnkey project. Designed as a 120-bed facility with the capacity to expand to 200 beds, the site is currently overgrown with weeds and its structures are deteriorating. While five other turnkey hospital projects—including the Dodowa District Hospital, Adansi North District Hospital at Fomena, Sekyere Kumawu District Hospital at Kumawu, and Garu Timpane Hospital in the Upper East Region—have been completed and operationalized, the Abetifi project has stalled, causing frustration among residents of Abetifi and surrounding communities.

The project was conceived around 2014 and 2015 during the tenure of Samuel Asamoah, the former District Chief Executive (DCE) for Kwahu East who is currently back in office. Asamoah stated that the Kwahu District Assembly secured the project land through traditional authorities, known as Nananom, who donated the land free of charge. In 2015, the contractor, NMS Infrastructure, moved to the site after the Ministry of Health compensated farmers for crops on the land to allow for construction. Work reportedly stalled following the 2016 change of government from the John Mahama-led National Democratic Congress (NDC) administration to the New Patriotic Party (NPP) government. At the time construction halted, the project was estimated to be between 35 and 40 per cent complete. Although NMS Infrastructure has maintained a presence at the site, there is no active construction.

cards.headline: Low-frequency rumbles reveal sophisticated communication among elephants in Namibia

pages.text: Behavioural ecologist Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell has spent 30 years studying African elephants in Namibia’s Etosha National Park, uncovering how low-frequency rumbles facilitate social bonds and leadership rituals. In a recent episode of the BBC Wildlife podcast Wild Lives, O'Connell-Rodwell described how these sounds function as a complex communication system used to coordinate group movements and resource sharing. These rumbles often occur at frequencies as low as 10Hz, which is below the threshold of human hearing and the capability of standard microphones, as humans can only detect sounds at least 30Hz.

O'Connell-Rodwell shared a recording of four male African elephants leaving a water hole, a process involving a ritual known as a “let’s go” rumble. In this interaction, a dominant individual invites the other three to leave the area. The group consisted of two tightly bonded pairs where, when one elephant rumbles, its partner responds accordingly. O'Connell-Rodwell noted that the elephants appear to manipulate their larynxes in a way that seems almost playful, with individuals adjusting their pitch in response to one another.

Research from the last 10 years indicates that these rituals among male elephants serve specific social functions. When a male elephant invites another to leave with him, it signals a willingness to share resources, such as acacia pods. This behavior demonstrates active leadership, as the individual initiating the rumble decides the direction the group will take while simultaneously expressing a desire for the other males to accompany him.

cards.headline: Niagara packaging business to move production to U.S. due to $500,000 weekly tariffs

pages.text: Stanpac, a family-owned packaging business in Niagara, Ontario, says 50 per cent tariffs are forcing the company to move production from Canada to the United States. Co-presidents Andrew Witt and Matt Witt stated the company is currently paying $500,000 per week in U.S. tariffs, an amount Andrew Witt said is much more than the company's profits. To mitigate the impact, the company is set to move specialized equipment used for producing plastic milk bottle lids and ice cream containers to its facilities in New Jersey and Texas. Stanpac manufactures packaging for ice cream brands such as Baskin-Robbins, Chapman’s, and Van Leeuwen.

Murray Bain, vice-president of marketing at Stanpac, told CBC News the company chose to absorb the tariff costs on Canadian goods crossing the border to keep prices stable and retain American customers against U.S.-based competitors. The company reported that the tariffs are billed and paid through its U.S. customs broker and taken directly from its account. While Stanpac requested relief from the federal Ministry of Industry, Bain noted there does not seem to be a clear path forward. The company's American sister facilities manufacture some products that are separate from and not subject to the 50 per cent tariffs the company is facing.

Founded in 1949, Stanpac operates six locations across North America. Since 1973, the company has been a major employer in Smithville, a community in West Lincoln where brothers Andrew and Matt Witt were raised.

cards.headline: At least 2,000 wild species live in homes across Canada and the U.S.

pages.text: Homes in Canada and the United States are inhabited by at least 2,000 wild species in addition to humans and pets, according to a study published in Ecology. The findings, which include everything from Asian lady beetles and a diverse range of spiders to the occasional alligator, suggest that indoor environments function as a growing ecosystem. Bradley Allf, an ecologist at Colorado State University who led the study, stated the findings demonstrate how humans are not separate from nature despite efforts to wall it out. Allf aimed to treat indoor spaces like a savannah or rainforest to understand the ecosystem within the habitat created by humans.

The study was conducted through a citizen science project called Never Home Alone, which utilized the iNaturalist app. In citizen science projects, members of the public participate in scientific research by collecting and sharing data. For this project, ordinary people submitted photos of wild species found indoors, which were then identified by a team of experts. Between 1996 and 2024, the project received more than 23,000 photos from 3,000 people across every U.S. state and every Canadian province, though not all territories.

Researchers noted that the bold jumping spider was one of the spiders commonly found in homes and submitted to the study, which Allf described as a surprise. Allf noted that the indoor environment contains ecological mysteries that remain largely unknown. While the study identifies a vast number of inhabitants, scientists suggest there are reasons why people should not put these found species outside.

cards.headline: Record 359,424 students in Japan did not attend school fully in fiscal 2025

pages.text: A record 359,424 elementary and junior high school students in Japan did not attend school fully during fiscal 2025, according to an annual report on student issues from the education ministry. The figure, which includes students at special needs schools, represents a 1.1% increase from the previous year and marks the 13th consecutive year of rising numbers. This total includes students who missed at least 30 school days during the school year without a stated cause, such as illness or financial issues. Over half of these students missed at least 90 separate days, and more than 10,000 students did not attend a single day. While the number of students has nearly tripled over the last decade, the rate of increase has shrunk significantly compared to the COVID-19 pandemic years, when the number of such students increased by as much as almost 25% at one period.

cards.headline: Thousands of women and girls report reproductive health issues following French police teargas use

pages.text: Almost 10,000 women and girls who participated in nationwide protests in October have provided testimony regarding disrupted menstrual cycles. Activists and health researchers fear that tens of thousands of women and young girls may have suffered immediate and long-term damage to their reproductive health due to heavy exposure to teargas used by French police during a wave of social protests that began in mid-September. On 17 October, at the height of the protests, French police fired approximately 22,000 teargas grenades at protesters, a rate equivalent to about two grenades every three seconds over 10 hours of maintaining order.

By early November, thousands of women across France were reporting symptoms similar to those described by Naïma Di Piero, a 46-year-old charity worker. Di Piero, who has endometriosis and uses the contraceptive pill to suppress her menstrual cycle, reported that two days after being exposed to teargas on 17 October, she began bleeding heavily. She stated that for 10 days her bleeding was so severe she had to change period underwear several times a day, followed by blood clots and debilitating cramps. Di Piero reported that the pain has disrupted her sleep, leaving her dependent on painkillers and a hot-water bottle, and she noted she is losing her hair.

There is limited scientific research linking teargas exposure to women’s health, as most past research has been conducted in military settings with healthy men. However, reports of women’s periods being affected by teargas have appeared during pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong in 2019, Black Lives Matter protests in the US in 2020, and during protests in Gaza and regarding immigration in 2024 and 2025.
